lesson.title: One Door, Many Rooms: The Accept Operation
lesson.summary: The accept operation pulls the next completed connection off a listening socket's backlog queue and hands back an entirely new socket dedicated to that one client, leaving the original listening socket free to keep listening.
lesson.body:
accept() is the call a server makes on a listening socket to retrieve the next completed connection waiting in the backlog queue that listen() set up.

The detail that trips up a lot of people learning this for the first time is what accept() actually returns. It does not hand back the listening socket itself. It returns a brand new socket, already connected to one specific client, while the original listening socket stays open and keeps right on listening for further incoming connections. That is exactly why a server can go on accepting new clients indefinitely: the listening socket's only job, forever, is to produce new per-client sockets, it never carries any actual data itself.

By default, accept() blocks, meaning it pauses the calling thread, until a connection is actually available to hand back. Many real servers either loop, calling accept() and handling one client at a time, or hand each newly accepted socket off to a separate thread or process so that multiple clients can be served at once, while the main loop immediately goes right back to calling accept() again for the next one.

accept() also typically hands back the remote client's socket address alongside the new socket, tying directly back to the earlier chapter on socket addresses, so the server always knows exactly who it is now talking to on that particular connection.

A concrete example pulls the whole TCP lifecycle together. A chat server calls socket(), binds to port 5000, and calls listen(). Three different clients call connect() to port 5000 one after another, at different times. Each of the server's three separate accept() calls returns a distinct new socket, one per client, so the server, whether using threads or some other approach, can read and write to client A's socket without any risk of it getting mixed up with client B's or client C's, even though all three connections arrived through that exact same listening socket on that exact same port.
